3: 8Scientific  RepoRts  |          (2019) 9:1194  | https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-018-37519-1
4: have maximum transparency. In vitro tests demonstrated good internalization of TiN NPs via endocytosis and an 
5: acceptable toxicity profile of laser-synthesized TiN NPs. Finally, we demonstrated a strong photothermal effect 
6: using laser-synthesized NPs as sensitizers of IR radiation-induced hyperthermia, comparable and even outper-
7: forming commercial TiN NPs. Altogether, our results demonstrate the potential of laser-synthesized TiN NPs as 
8: a photoabsorbing agent for further photothermal studies in vivo.
9: Methods
10: synthesis of nanoparticles. TiN NPs were synthesized by ultra-shot (fs) laser ablation of bulk TiN target 
11: in liquid medium at ambient conditions, similar to how it was done in our previous papers 30–32. Briefly, hot-
12: pressed TiN target (GoodFellow) was placed on the bottom of a glass vessel filled with 7 mL of ultrapure water 
13: (18.2 MΩ cm at 25 °C) or acetone (analytical reagent grade, Fisher Chemical), as shown in Fig. 1a. The liquid layer 
14: above the target was 10 mm thick. A 2.3 mm diameter beam from a Yb:KGW laser (Amplitude Systems, 1025 nm, 
15: 1–100 kHz) was focused by a 75 mm lens on the surface of the target. To account for shifts of the focal position 
16: due to non-linear effects, accompanying the interaction of intense fs pulse with liquid, we adjusted the lens – tar-
17: get distance to achieve maximum productivity (maximum ablated mass per a time period). This adjustment was 
18: especially important for acetone, as in the case of acetone ambience the change of pulse energy from 10 mJ to 100 
19: mJ led to a shift of lens position by 10 mm. The target was continuously moved at a speed of 2 mm s
20: −1  during the 
21: ablation step to avoid ablation from the same point.
22: As an additional method to control TiN NPs size we used a technique of fs laser fragmentation, which was 
23: developed in our previous works34–36. The experimental setup for laser fragmentation is shown in Fig. 1b. Briefly, 
24: colloidal solutions of TiN NPs, which were preliminary prepared by laser ablation step, were exposed to radiation 
25: of the same laser in the absence of the target. The laser beam was focused with the help of a 75 mm lens at 1 cm 
26: below the liquid surface. The solution was continuously homogenized by a magnetic stirrer during the fragmen-
27: tation process.
28: To minimize oxidation effects during ablation and fragmentation processes, in some cases we pumped out 
29: oxygen dissolved in solutions by bubbling them with Ar gas before and during the experiments similarly to how 
30: it was done in our previous works
31: 44.
32: Figure 7. TEM images of endosomes containing TiN NPs (marked by arrows), observed after exposure of 
33: U87–MG spheroids to 1 μg mL−1  of TiN NPs for 10 days.
34: Figure 8. Area (blue marks) and viability (red marks) of U87–MG cells spheroids as a function of (a) TiN NPs 
35: concentration and (b) laser exposure time. Insets demonstrate corresponding bright-field photomicrographs.

41: Characterization of nanoparticles. Morphology, structure and size of synthesized NPs were character-
42: ized by the high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HR-TEM) system (JEOL JEM 3010) operating at 
43: 300 kV and equipped with a Gatan Multiscan CCD in imaging and diffraction modes. Samples were prepared by 
44: dropping 5 μL of NPs solution onto a carbon-coated TEM copper grid and subsequent drying at ambient con-
45: ditions. Analysis of selected area electron diffraction (SAED) patterns was performed using ProcessDiffraction 
46: v.8.7.1 software45 Uncertainty in determination of lattice constants was estimated as full width at half maximum 
47: (FWHM) of diffraction rings after lognormal correction for background signal. ζ–potential measurements were 
48: performed using a Zetasizer ZS instrument (Malvern Instruments, Orsay, France). Extinction spectra of NPs 
49: solutions were measured by a UV– VIS spectrophotometer (UV–2600, Shimadzu) using 10 mm optical path 
50: length quartz cuvettes. Concentrations of NPs solutions were determined by measuring target weight before and 
51: after the ablation step. As the TiN target was produced by hot-pressing of a TiN powder and presented a porous 
52: material, a prolonged drying step was required to determine the mass change correctly. Additional concentration 
53: measurements were done using the inductively coupled plasma – mass spectrometry (ICP–MS) method.
54: Cell cultures.  Safety of TiN NPs was evaluated on 2D culture of human microvascular endothelial cells 
55: (HMEC–1) and 2D and 3D cultures of human glioblastoma cancer cells (U87–MG). Cells were obtained from 
56: American Type Culture Collection (Manassas, V A, USA). HMEC–1 cells were maintained in MCDB 131 medium 
57: (Gibco, UK) containing 10% of decomplemented fetal bovine serum, 2 mM L–Glutamine (Gibco, UK), 1% (v/v) 
58: of penicillin/streptomycin solution (Gibco, UK) and 0.1% of epidermal growth factor. U87–MG cells were main-
59: tained in EMEM (Lonza, Verviers, Belgium) supplemented with 10% of decomplemented fetal bovine serum, 
60: 2mM L–Glutamine and 1% (v/v) of penicillin/streptomycin.
61: Viability assay using 2D cell cultures. 3000 cells for HMEC–1 and 4000 cells for U87–MG were seeded 
62: on 96 – well plates and kept at 37 °C in a humidified incubator filled with 5% CO2. After 24 h of growth, culture 
63: medium was replaced by 150 μL of fresh medium containing different concentrations of TiN NPs ranging from 
64: 0.025 to 10 μg mL− 1. After a 72 h of incubation cell viability was assessed using resazurin reduction protocol: 15 μL 
65: of resazurin reagent (alamarBlue, Thermo Fisher Scientific) was added to each well, and incubated for 6 h before 
66: fluorescence was measured by a microplate reader (POLARstar Omega, BMG LABTECH). All fluorescence data 
67: were corrected by subtraction of the background signal from blank wells. Viability was calculated as a fluores-
68: cence signal from a sample, normalized to the fluorescence signal from control wells not subjected to TiN NPs. 
69: Experiments were repeated three times independently, with four wells for each experimental condition.
70: Viability assay using 3D cell cultures.  To obtain U87–MG cells 3D culture in a form of spheroids, 
71: cells growing in regular 2D cultures were rinsed once in phosphate buffered saline, then detached using 0.02% 
72: Trypsin/EDTA (Gibco, UK), pelleted by centrifugation at 200 g for 5 min and finally resuspended in a fresh cul-
73: ture medium supplemented with 20% methylcellulose and seeded on round-bottom 96 – well plates (Greiner 
74: Bio–one, Courtaboeuf, France) at 1000 cells per well in 100 μL of medium. After 72 h of growth at 37 °C under 
75: 5% CO
76: 2 spheroids were formed and 100 μL of fresh medium containing different amounts of TiN NPs with final 
77: concentrations from 0.1 to 15 μg mL−1  were added to wells. The spheroids growth was maintained for 13 days by 
78: adding 10 μL of fresh medium per well three times a week and was monitored daily by measuring spheroid area 
79: on bright–field photomicrographs (Eclipse Ts2–FL, Nikon). All images were segmented using a custom macro 
80: script, written for ImageJ software
81: 46. At day 13 of exposure to TiN NPs cell viability was assessed by the resazurin 
82: reduction protocol as described above for 2D cell culture, but with 20  μL of resazurin reagent per well and 18 h 
83: of incubation.
84: Assay of nanoparticles cell uptake. TiN NPs uptake in spheroids of U87–MG cells was studied by trans-
85: mission electron microscope (JEOL, Japan) operating at 80 kV and equipped with Megaview III camera. Six 
86: spheroids exposed to 1 μg mL− 1 of TiN NPs for 10 days were fixed with 2.5% glutaraldehyde in 0.1 M sodium 
87: cacodylate buffer for 40 min, then washed again. Samples were progressively dehydrated with 50% to 100% etha-
88: nol bathes, before being embedded in epoxy resin (EPON 812) with a series of bathes ranging from 33% to 100% 
89: resin, and overnight polymerization at 55 °C. 60 nm sections of spheroids were obtained using Ultracut-E ultra-
90: microtome (Reichert–Jung, USA) and contrasted by incubation in 5% uranyl acetate.
91: Photothermal therapy tests on 3D cell cultures.  Photothermal effect of TiN NPs was studied by 
92: exposing spheroids of U87–MG cells to different concentrations of TiN NPs for four days before laser treatment. 
93: The wells were fully filled by the culture medium and sealed with a semi-permeable membrane (Breathe–Easy, 
94: Diversified Biotech, Dedham, MA, USA) before laser exposure to avoid condensation on the microplate lids. 
95: Spheroids were irradiated by continuous-wave (CW) laser (SLD1332V , 670 nm, 500 mW , Thorlabs) with an inten-
96: sity of 4.4 W cm
97: −2  (310 mW power, 3 mm beam diameter) for different exposure times varying from 1 to 15 min. 
98: Spheroids area and viability were measured as described above.

input.content:
# L1 — часть 03 (с. 8–11 PDF)

[порождено] Часть охватывает с. 8–11 PDF. Синтез: абляция массивной мишени TiN фемтосекундным лазером (Yb:KGW, 1025 нм, 1–100 кГц, пучок 2,3 мм, линза 75 мм) в 7 мл воды (18,2 МОм·см при 25 °C) или ацетона; слой жидкости 10 мм, мишень движется 2 мм/с (с. 8). Фрагментация — облучение коллоида тем же лазером без мишени, фокус на 1 см ниже поверхности, магнитная мешалка; иногда кислород удаляли барботированием Ar (с. 8). Методы: HR-TEM 300 кВ, ζ-потенциал, UV-VIS, ICP-MS (с. 9). Цитотоксичность: HMEC-1 и U87-MG в 2D (0,025–10 мкг/мл, 72 ч) и сфероиды U87-MG (0,1–15 мкг/мл, 13 сут); фотогермия: CW 670 нм, 4,4 Вт/см² (310 мВт, 3 мм), 1–15 мин (с. 9). На с. 8 указано изменение энергии «from 10 mJ to 100 mJ»; это не согласуется с фс-режимом, противоречие не разрешаю без источника. Данные in vitro не означают результата лечения людей.

## Цитаты для сверки

[источник] «ultra-shot (fs) laser ablation of bulk TiN target in liquid medium at ambient conditions» — с. 8.

[источник] «the change of pulse energy from 10 mJ to 100 mJ led to a shift of lens position by 10 mm» — с. 8.

[источник] «intensity of 4.4 W cm−2 (310 mW power, 3 mm beam diameter) for different exposure times varying from 1 to 15 min» — с. 9.
